# Guarantee Taxonomy — Reversing Risk

**Source:** *$100M Offers*, "Enhancing Your Offer: Guarantees" (lines ~2383–2613).
The 4th enhancer. **Risk is "the single greatest objection for any product or service"** (l.2389), so
reversing it is the fastest way to make any offer more attractive — Jason Fladlien saw conversion
**2–4x** just by changing the *quality* of the guarantee (l.2391). Spend a disproportionate amount of
time crafting it.

> "You must *always* hit your guarantee hard, even if you don't have one." (l.2403) — say it boldly and
> give the reason why.

---

## The guarantee formula (what gives it teeth) (l.2423–2431)

> **"If you do not get X result in Y time period, we will Z."**

The power is in the **conditional statement** — you must decide *what you'll do if they don't get the
result*. Without the "or what" ("Z"), a guarantee "sounds weak and diluted" — which is what most
marketers do.
- **Bad:** "We will get you 20 clients guaranteed."
- **Better:** "You will get 20 clients in your first 30 days, or we give you your money back + your
  advertising dollars spent with us." (l.2431)

## "Won't people take advantage?" — do the math (l.2405–2415)
Sometimes, but rarely — and the math still wins. *Worked pattern (his own numbers, l.2409–2411):*
100 sales / 5 refunds = 95 net; a stronger guarantee → 130 sales / 13 refunds (refund rate *doubled*
5%→10%) = 117 net → **117/95 = 1.23x (23% more), all to the bottom line.** For a guarantee to *not* be
worth it, the sales lift would have to be 100% offset by refunds — unlikely. **"Don't be emotional,
just do the math."**
- **Warning (l.2415):** people who buy *because* of a guarantee can become "very shitty customers" —
  they may not do the work. Tie the guarantee to the actions needed for success to protect both parties.
- **Pro Tip — High-Cost Services Warning (l.2417–2419):** if fulfillment cost is high, prefer a
  **conditional** or **anti-guarantee** — otherwise you eat the refund *and* the cost of fulfilling.

---

## The four categories (l.2393–2449)

Ordered strongest → most protective of you. **Unconditional is the strongest.**

### 1) Unconditional (l.2435–2437)
The strongest. Essentially a **trial — they pay first, then see if they like it.** Gets a LOT more
people to buy; you *will* get some refunds. No conditions to qualify.

### 2) Conditional (l.2439–2441)
Includes **"terms and conditions."** Where you get *very* creative. Aim for **"better than money back"**
— match the buyer's investment with an equal-or-higher perceived commitment. Bake in the **key actions
someone must take to succeed** — in a perfect world 100% qualify but have already gotten the result, so
they don't want it. (Given the choice of a refund vs. the promised outcome, most take the outcome.)

### 3) Anti-Guarantee (l.2443–2445)
Explicitly **"all sales are final."** Own the position with a creative **"reason why"** — typically a
massive exposure/vulnerability on your part the consumer instantly understands. Especially for items
**consumable or that massively diminish in value once given.**

### 4) Implied (l.2447–2449)
Any **performance-based** offer — revshare, profitshare, triggers, ratchets, monetary bonuses. Concept:
**"if I don't perform, I don't get paid"** (plus the upside "if I do great, I'm well compensated").
Only works with **transparency to measure the outcome** and **trust/control that you'll be paid** when
you perform.

---

## Every named guarantee, by category

### [Unconditional] "No Questions Asked" Refund Guarantee (l.2461–2465)
**Client gets one of:** A) a full refund · B) a 50% refund · C) a refund of their ad spend + any
ancillary costs incurred · D) you pay for a competitor's program instead · E) return their money **plus
an additional $1,000** (or applicable amount).
**Take:** simplest and riskiest — you're accountable whether or not the miss is your fault. Adding
conditions weakens it fast.

### [Unconditional] Satisfaction-Based Refund Guarantee (l.2479–2489)
**Client gets:** if at *any time* they're not satisfied with the level of service, they can request a
refund (at any time).
**Take:** the **highest form of guarantee** — you could do everything right and they can still refund.
Works much better **lower-ticket**; risky as fulfillment cost rises. (His weight-loss version: two
takers out of 4,000 sales in 3.5 years.)

### [Conditional] Outsized Refund Guarantee (l.2495–2501)
**Client gets:** **double or triple their money back**, or a no-strings payment of $X,XXX (far more
than they paid).
**Take:** for **high-margin** products, paired with a **consumption condition** (they must do things to
qualify). *(Fladlien pattern: "spend $X on ads using these methods and don't make money → I buy your
store for $25,000" — reportedly $3M extra sales, only 10 refunds paid.)*

### [Conditional] Service Guarantee (l.2503–2515)
**Client gets:** you **keep working for them free of charge until X is achieved.**
**Take:** Hormozi's "personal favorite" — guarantees the outcome, eliminates *time* as a risk; you never
risk the money because the guarantee is around the outcome. Condition it on success-linked actions
(attend calls, weigh in, report data).

### [Conditional] Modified Service Guarantee (l.2517–2521)
**Client gets:** another **Y-long period** of service/access free of charge (Y ≈ at least **twice the
duration**).
**Take:** like the Service Guarantee but time-boxed — you're on the hook for a *finite* period, an
easier place to start than the "all-out" version.

### [Conditional] Credit-Based Guarantee (l.2523–2527)
**Client gets:** what they paid back **as a credit toward any service you offer** (not cash).
**Take:** best during an **upsell** to seal a service they're unsure about — worst case they apply it to
what they already like; maintains goodwill.

### [Conditional] Personal Service Guarantee (l.2529–2533)
**Client gets:** you work with them **one-on-one, free of charge, until they reach X.**
**Take:** "a service guarantee on crack" — one of the strongest in existence. **Definitely add
conditions** (respond within 24h, use the prescribed products, etc.). More powerful as you become more
edified.

### [Conditional] Hotel + Airfare Perks Guarantee (l.2535–2539)
**Client gets:** if they don't receive value, you reimburse the product **+ their hotel + airfare.**
**Take:** a "refund of ancillary costs" variant; great for **workshops/in-person** events — tangible,
original, ~like adding $1,000 to the guarantee.

### [Conditional] Wage-Payment Guarantee (l.2541–2545)
**Client gets:** you pay **their hourly rate** if they don't find your call/session valuable.
**Take:** an original ancillary-cost guarantee. (If anyone asks: divide their tax return by 1,960 hrs —
but no one refunding will actually do that, so you'll "never actually have to give one out.")

### [Conditional] Release of Service Guarantee (l.2547–2551)
**Client gets:** you **let them out of their contract** free of charge.
**Take:** voids a commitment/cancellation fee. Powerful if you have enforceable contracts — and *free*
to offer if you don't enforce them anyway.

### [Conditional] Delayed Second Payment Guarantee (l.2553–2557)
**Client gets:** you **won't bill them again until *after* they get their first outcome** (lose first 5
lbs, make first sale, get website live).
**Take:** gets the prospect thinking fast-action; focuses your team on activating the client; great when
you know the metric that predicts long-term retention.

### [Conditional] First Outcome Guarantee (l.2559–2563)
**Client gets:** you **keep paying their ancillary costs (ad spend, hotel, etc.) until they reach their
first outcome.** *(Ex: no first sale in 14 days → we pay your ad spend until you do.)*
**Take:** like Delayed Second Payment but centered on a cost; keeps everyone focused on the first dollar
over the bridge.

### [Anti-Guarantee] All Sales Are Final (l.2565–2573)
**Client gets:** access to a **super-exclusive, very valuable** service/product — something that "once
seen cannot be unseen, or once used cannot be taken away" (a line of code, cold-open scripts).
**Take:** a **damaging admission** — implies the client *will* benefit, exposing you to vulnerability.
**Requires a strong "reason why"** ("our process is so powerful that once used it can't be unused").
Also works for high-ticket, high-customization work ("if you need a guarantee before jumping, you're
not who we want to work with").

### [Implied] Performance / Revshare / Profit-Share (l.2575–2591)
- **Performance:** A) $XXX per sale / $XXX per show · B) $XX per lb lost.
- **Revshare:** A) 10% of top-line revenue · B) 20% profit share · C) 25% of revenue growth from baseline.
- **Profit-Share:** A) X% of profit · B) X% of gross profit.
- **Ratchets:** 10% if over X, 20% if over Y, 30% if over Z.
- **Bonuses/Triggers:** I get X when Y occurs.
**Client gets:** if you don't perform, they don't pay; if you perform, comp is per an agreement set
*before* work begins.
**Take:** Hormozi's favorite setup — accountability to results, weeds out low performers, aligns both
sides. Drawbacks: **tracking and collection.** Can pair with a **minimum** ("the greater of $1,000 or
10% of revenue") or a ramp ("$1,000/mo for 3 months, then 100% performance").

---

## Stacking Guarantees (l.2451–2455)
Like bonuses, guarantees **stack**:
- **Unconditional + Conditional:** e.g. an unconditional 30-day no-questions-asked guarantee, *plus* a
  conditional triple-your-money-back 90-day guarantee.
- **Two conditionals around sequential outcomes:** "You'll make $10,000 by 60 days, $30,000 by 90 days,
  as long as you do things 1, 2, and 3." This **future-paces** the prospect into believing the outcome
  and shifts the burden of risk back onto you.

## Name your guarantee something cool (l.2471–2477)
Don't use "satisfaction" or vanilla words — describe it more strongly with creative imagery.
- **Bad:** "30 Day Money Back Satisfaction Guarantee."
- **Good:** "In 30 days, if you wouldn't jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we
  return every dollar."
- **Great:** the "**Club a Baby Seal Guarantee**" — "after 30 days, if you wouldn't club a baby seal to
  stay a customer, you don't pay a penny."

---

## Decision rule — which guarantee fits which business

**Primary lever: ticket size × fulfillment cost × B2C-vs-B2B** (l.2489–2493, 2417–2419):

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| **Lower-ticket B2C** (many won't bother refunding) | Bigger, broader **Unconditional** (No-Questions / Satisfaction). |
| **Higher-ticket, business-oriented** | Steer toward **specific / Conditional** — may or may not include refunds or conditions. |
| **High fulfillment cost** | **Conditional** or **Anti-Guarantee** (don't eat refund *and* fulfillment). |
| **High margins + you need the client to do a lot** | **Conditional Outsized Refund** with a consumption condition. |
| **You can measure the outcome + trust you'll be paid** | **Implied / Performance** (strongest alignment). |
| **Consumable / value diminishes once seen** | **Anti-Guarantee** (all sales final + a strong reason why). |
| **Upsell of a service they're unsure about** | **Credit-Based.** |

**Hormozi's starting advice (l.2601):** *start* with **service-based guarantees or performance
partnerships** — this makes all sales final (no refund fear) and commits you to the client's results.
From there, keep it and scale, or move "up the food chain" to less restrictive guarantees to increase
volume.

## Create Your Own (l.2593–2599)
Identify the client's **biggest fears, pain, and perceived obstacles** — "What do they *not* want to
have happen if they pay you? What are they most afraid of?" — and **reverse those fears into a
guarantee.** The more specific and creative, the better. *Caveat:* guarantees are **enhancers, not a
business** — used to cover a poor product/sales team, they backfire into refunds.

---

## Output contract for `hormozi-offer-guarantees`

For *this* product, produce:
1. **1–2 chosen guarantees** (or a **stack**), selected via the decision table above — name the
   category (Unconditional / Conditional / Anti / Implied) and the specific named type.
2. Each written in the **"If you don't get X in Y, we do Z"** structure, with X/Y/Z filled from the
   product's real dream outcome, timeframe, and economics (or `<placeholder>` — **no fabricated
   numbers**), plus any **consumption conditions** (the success-linked actions).
3. A **cool name** (creative imagery, not "satisfaction").
4. A one-line **basis** — why this category fits this ticket size / fulfillment cost / B2C-vs-B2B.

## Sources and basis

*$100M Offers* — risk as top objection + 2–4x (l.2389–2391), "always hit it hard" (l.2403), four types
(l.2393–2449), the math (l.2405–2415), High-Cost Pro Tip (l.2417–2419), the formula + Bad/Better
(l.2423–2431), every named guarantee (Unconditional l.2461–2489; Conditional l.2495–2563;
Anti-Guarantee l.2565–2573; Implied l.2575–2591), Stacking (l.2451–2455), Name-It-Cool (l.2471–2477),
Unconditional-vs-Conditional by business type (l.2491–2493), Create Your Own (l.2593–2601).
